Revenue models for long cycles

Playbooklowob research

By lowob · 31 August 2026 · 8-minute read · Revenue

In short: Pick the revenue model by who carries the capital and the service tail, price pilots and production differently, and report only what would survive due diligence. The revenue model also decides how the company is financed. US federal energy lenders, for example, prefer technology at readiness level 8, deny pilot and demonstration projects and look for contracted cash flows, so the contract terms you write today decide whether your fiftieth unit is funded by debt or by more dilution.

Key points

  • Every model answers one question: who carries the capital and who carries the risk of the thing not working.
  • Hardware-as-a-service works only with a financing partner behind it; otherwise each unit consumes equity.
  • Gross margin per unit including the measured service tail is the number that decides whether any model works.
  • Project lenders want proven designs and contracted cash flows: US federal energy loans cannot exceed 80% of eligible project costs and typically run $500 million or more.
  • Stop reporting letters of intent and pipeline value; report converted pilots, contracted annual value and margin including service.

Five models, one question

Every emerging tech revenue model answers the same question: who carries the capital and who carries the risk of the thing not working. Match the model to the answer your buyer and your balance sheet can live with.

Hardware plus service is the default. The buyer pays for the unit upfront and a recurring fee for software, monitoring, maintenance and updates. Capital sits with the buyer. Your margin is visible on day one. The weakness is that the upfront price triggers capex approval, which is often the slowest door in the building.

Hardware-as-a-service moves the unit onto your balance sheet and charges a monthly or annual fee. The buyer's capex problem disappears. Yours appears. This model works only with financing behind it: equipment finance, a leasing partner or a project finance vehicle. Without that, every unit you deploy consumes equity, and the runway maths in Raising for long cycles breaks.

Outcome or usage pricing charges per inspection, per kWh delivered, per verification, per task completed. It aligns you with the buyer completely. It also requires two things most early companies lack: a measurement the buyer trusts and enough deployment history to price the risk. Use it only when both exist, and expect to start with a floor fee. Our explainer on outcome-based pricing covers the same trade-off in software.

Licensing and royalties suit IP-heavy companies with an OEM route, as Integrators, OEMs and channel partners described. Low margin per unit, no service tail, wide reach. Pair a licence fee with a per-unit royalty and a minimum commitment.

Network or token models apply to DePIN and only if the test in Token or no token is passed: the token must do a job the network cannot do without it. If it fails that test, it is a financing mechanism dressed as a revenue model and will be priced as one.

ModelWho carries capitalService tail riskNeeds
Hardware plus serviceBuyerYou, priced inClear unit economics
Hardware-as-a-serviceYouYouFinancing partner
Outcome or usageYouYouTrusted measurement
Licence and royaltyOEMOEMProtected IP, minimums
Network or tokenNetworkOperatorsThe token test passed

Gross margin and the service tail

The number that decides whether any of this works is gross margin per unit including the service tail. Not hardware margin. Not software margin. The blended number after field service, spares, remote monitoring, firmware support and the hours a customer success engineer spends on site.

Most emerging tech companies know their bill of materials and guess their service cost. Measure it from the first deployment. Log every site visit, every spare, every support hour against the unit it served. After ten units you will have a real number. It will be worse than the model. That is fine. Price the next contracts on it, using value-based pricing where the buyer's saving is measurable.

Before a deployment passes its success test, the unit is research. After, it is a financeable asset.

Project finance or equity

Raising for long cycles covered the capital stack. The revenue model decides which layer pays for what.

Equity pays for things that reduce technical and commercial risk: engineering, the first deployments, the playbook. Project finance or asset finance pays for things that are already de-risked: the fiftieth unit of a design that has run for a year at three sites. Using equity to fund fleet deployment is the most common and most expensive mistake in this vertical. Using debt before the design is stable is the second.

Lenders state the line plainly. Mayer Brown's August 2026 guide to the US Office of Energy Dominance Financing, formerly the Loan Programs Office, says projects must use technically viable and commercially ready technology, with a preferred technology readiness level of 8, and that research, pilot or demonstration projects will be denied. It advises applicants to consider long-term offtake agreements or other contracted cash flows, notes that sponsors must contribute significant equity, and says loans cannot exceed 80% of eligible project costs, with debt typically covering 40% to 60% and direct loans typically $500 million or more. Most startups will never borrow at that scale, but private equipment lenders ask the same questions at smaller sizes.

Public grant programmes draw a similar line earlier. The EU's EIC Accelerator offers grants from technology readiness level 6 to 8 and reserves its equity for market entry at level 9. In the US, the SBIR Strategic Breakthrough awards created in April 2026, worth up to $30 million, go only to companies with a prior Phase II award and must be matched dollar for dollar by new private capital or other funds. Investors are funding the category: Carta's platform data shows hardware capital rising from $8.6 billion to $14.3 billion between the first halves of 2025 and 2026. But each source funds a specific stage of proof.

Stage of proofWhat funds it wellWhat the revenue contract must show
Lab to first field unitGrants, seed equityNothing yet; a defined success test
Paid pilotEquity, pilot feesFixed fee, scope, success test, conversion price
First production contractsEquity, strategic capitalTerm, minimums, service level
Fleet deploymentEquipment, asset or project financeContracted cash flows a lender can underwrite

The line between equity and debt is the same success test from First customers in a market that doesn't exist yet. Once a deployment has passed it, the unit is a financeable asset. Before that, it is research.

Pilots as projects, production as contracts

Price a pilot as a project. Fixed scope, fixed fee, fixed duration, a defined success test and a stated conversion price if it passes. The fee should cover your cost. A free pilot teaches the buyer that your product is worth nothing and teaches you nothing about their procurement.

Price production as a contract with a term. A minimum number of units or sites, a minimum duration, a service level, a renewal clause and an exit cost. The term is what makes contracted annual value a real number and what makes the business financeable, because it is the contracted cash flow a lender reads.

Never let a pilot drift into production on pilot terms. Set the conversion date in the pilot agreement. Our guide to pricing experiments in B2B covers how to test a conversion price without discounting the first contracts away.

What to report, and what to stop

Stop reporting reach said report what happened, not who saw it. For emerging tech, the equivalent is to stop reporting intent.

ReportStop reporting
Paid pilots converted to contracts, as a count and a rateLetters of intent
Contracted annual value, with termPipeline value
Gross margin per unit including serviceHardware margin alone
Deployment lead time from signature to commissioningUnits "ordered" with no deposit or delivery date
Performance against the success test, per siteDemo results
Risk retired this quarter, in plain wordsCategory size

Each item in the right-hand column is a story about the future. Investors have heard the story. Customers never see it. Neither will pay for it. The left-hand column is what a board can trust, as our guide to commercial KPIs a board will trust sets out.

Closing the series

This piece closed the emerging tech section of Raise, Rally, Revenue. The spine applies everywhere: one system, one product truth, evidence before the raise, a round run like a sales process, community with a job, design partners, distribution built because the platforms are closed, measurement instead of reach, and a company that runs without you. Each vertical changes who buys, what proof counts, which channels are open and what to measure. The whole series on one page sets out the order and the vertical table, and How to raise for an emerging tech company brings the fundraising parts together.

The order matters more than any tactic. Every failure we have seen in this series came from doing a right thing at the wrong time.

lowob takeaways

  • Choose the model by who carries capital and the service tail. Then check your balance sheet can carry your part.
  • Measure service cost from unit one. Gross margin including service is the number that decides.
  • Write contracts a lender can read. Terms, minimums and contracted cash flows turn units into financeable assets.
  • Report what happened. Converted pilots and contracted annual value, never intent.

Common questions

How should a hardware startup price a pilot?

As a project with fixed scope, fee and duration, a defined success test and a stated conversion price. The fee should cover cost, and the conversion date should be set in the pilot agreement.

When does hardware-as-a-service make sense?

Only with financing behind it, such as equipment finance, a leasing partner or a project finance vehicle, and only for a design that has passed its success test. Without that, every deployed unit consumes equity.

Should deep tech companies use equity or project finance for deployments?

Equity should fund what reduces technical and commercial risk. Project or asset finance should fund units of a proven design with contracted cash flows; US federal energy lenders, for example, deny pilot and demonstration projects.

What should emerging tech companies report to their board?

Converted pilots as a count and rate, contracted annual value with term, gross margin per unit including service, deployment lead time, performance against the success test and risk retired. Not letters of intent or pipeline value.
